tables.sourceText: Term What it means Substance use A person consumes a substance. This alone does not establish dependence or a medical diagnosis. Harmful or risky use Use that increases the chance of injury or contributes to health, social or other harm. Harm may occur without dependence. Substance use disorder A recognized health condition involving a problematic pattern of use, assessed by qualified professionals using established criteria.

tables.sourceText: System Potential effects or health concerns Brain and nerves Impaired attention, memory, motor coordination; long-term heavy use can damage nervous tissue. Liver and digestion Risk of liver disease and digestive or pancreatic conditions. Heart and circulation High blood pressure, irregular heart rhythm and other cardiovascular conditions. Cancer risk Alcohol increases risk for several cancers, including breast, liver and colorectal cancers. Relationships and safety Injury, interpersonal harm, road crashes, school or work difficulties.

tables.sourceText: Substance group Possible immediate problems Possible longer-term concerns Opioids Sleepiness and slowed breathing; overdose can be fatal. Dependence and overdose risk, especially with unregulated products or sedative combinations. Stimulants Agitation, elevated heart rate, overheating, high blood pressure. Cardiovascular, sleep and mental-health difficulties; stimulant use disorder may develop. Sedatives Drowsiness, poor coordination and potentially dangerous interactions. Dependence and hazardous withdrawal with some medicines; requires clinical supervision. Cannabis Impaired attention, memory, coordination; possible anxiety or paranoia. Cannabis use disorder; in some people, cognitive and mental-health concerns, especially with frequent early use. Inhalants Unpredictable toxic effects; fainting, abnormal heartbeat or sudden death. Potential neurological, liver or kidney damage with some exposures.

tables.sourceText: Myth Better explanation “Only addicted people are harmed.” A single exposure can cause injury or poisoning without dependence. “Beer is safer because it is common.” Beer contains ethanol; amount consumed matters, and no alcoholic drink is risk-free. “A prescription medicine is safe to share.” Prescriptions are individualized; sharing or combining medicines can be dangerous. “Everyone who uses drugs becomes addicted.” Not everyone develops a disorder, but serious risks may still occur. “A person who looks awake can drive safely.” Appearance and confidence do not reliably indicate unimpaired judgment or reaction time.

“A prescription medicine is safe to share.”
Prescriptions are individualized; sharing or combining medicines can be dangerous.
“Everyone who uses drugs becomes addicted.”
Not everyone develops a disorder, but serious risks may still occur.
“A person who looks awake can drive safely.”
Appearance and confidence do not reliably indicate unimpaired judgment or reaction time.

tables.sourceText: Question Model answer Can injury happen without addiction? Yes. Impairment, poisoning or accidents may occur without a substance use disorder. Do all drugs have identical effects? No. Their mechanisms, acute dangers and longer-term risks differ. Does every person who drinks develop liver disease? No. Risks vary; not everyone develops a disease, and serious risk still warrants prevention. Is quitting heavy alcohol use always safe without advice? No. Physically dependent people can experience dangerous withdrawal. What matters most in a possible overdose? Prompt emergency help and attention to breathing and consciousness.
